title: Read an Academic Passage
lines: Read an Academic Passage is the closest task to university reading. You get a passage of about 200 words from a textbook-style source on a topic such as ecology, geology, art history, psychology or business, and five questions about it. You do not need any background knowledge: everything you need is in the passage, and outside knowledge can even mislead you.
## What is on the screen
- The passage, usually one or two paragraphs. Long passages can be scrolled.
- Five multiple-choice questions, one at a time or in a list, each with four options.
- Some questions highlight a word or sentence in the passage so you can find it fast.
## Timing

The task is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for the whole section). Plan about 4 to 5 minutes per passage: 1.5 to 2 minutes to read, then about 30-40 seconds per question. If a question is taking too long, choose the best option and move on.
## Question types
- Main idea: What is the passage mainly about? What is the main point of the paragraph?
- Detail: According to the passage, what ...?
- Negative fact: All of the following are mentioned EXCEPT ...
- Vocabulary in context: The word "X" in the passage is closest in meaning to ...
- Reference: The word "it" or "this" in the passage refers to ...
- Inference: What can be inferred about ...?
- Purpose: Why does the author mention ...? What is the purpose of the second sentence?
- Organization: How is the information in the passage organized?
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the first sentence and the last sentence of the passage first. Together they usually show the topic and the main point.

- Step 2: Read the whole passage once, building a quick mental map: claim, explanation, example, contrast, conclusion. Notice signal words: however, for example, as a result, in contrast, in addition, this suggests.
- Step 3: Answer the main idea question with the map, not with one sentence. The correct answer covers the whole passage.
- Step 4: For detail, negative fact and reference questions, go back to the exact place. For reference questions, put each option in place of the pronoun and check the sentence still makes sense.
- Step 5: For vocabulary questions, use the sentence, not your memory. Substitute each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.
- Step 6: For purpose questions, ask what job the sentence or example does: support a claim, give a contrast, define a term, show an exception.
- Step 7: For inference, choose what the passage strongly supports. Reject options that go further than the text.
## Worked example 1

> Many desert plants survive long dry periods by storing water in thick stems or leaves. Cacti are the best-known example: their stems can swell after rain and shrink slowly as the water is used. Other species take a different approach. Instead of storing water, they avoid drought altogether by completing their life cycle quickly. After a rare heavy rain, their seeds germinate, the plants flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks, and then the adults die. The seeds may then wait in the soil for years until the next good rain. A third group relies on very deep roots that reach water far below the surface. These strategies show that there is no single solution to life in a dry climate.
> Question: What is the passage mainly about?
> A. Why cacti are the most successful desert plants
> B. Different ways in which plants deal with a lack of water
> C. How desert seeds can survive for many years
> D. The effect of heavy rain on desert soil

B matches the map: storing water, avoiding drought, deep roots, and the conclusion "no single solution". A is too narrow and too extreme ("most successful" is not stated). C is one detail. D is not discussed.
> Question: Why does the author mention cacti?
> A. To give a familiar example of the first strategy
> B. To argue that storing water is the best strategy
> C. To contrast them with plants that have deep roots
> D. To explain why some seeds wait for years
A: the passage says cacti are "the best-known example" of storing water. Purpose questions ask about the job of the detail; here the job is illustration.
> Question: What can be inferred about the plants that complete their life cycle quickly?
> A. They grow larger than cacti.
> B. Their adult plants are rarely seen during dry years.
> C. They need deep roots to survive.
> D. They store water in their seeds.

B follows from the text: the adults die after a few weeks, and the seeds wait until the next good rain, so in dry years there are few or no adult plants. A and D are not supported; C belongs to the third group.
## Worked example 2

> Visitors who see ancient Egyptian wall paintings for the first time often think the artists lacked skill, because the figures look flat and stiff. Historians of art see it differently. Egyptian painters were usually not trying to copy what the eye sees from one position. A person was often shown with the face in profile but the eye and shoulders from the front, so that each part appeared in its clearest, most recognizable view. Size followed the same logic: an important official might be painted much larger than the servants around him to show his rank, not his height. From this point of view, the apparent "errors" were deliberate choices that served the purpose of the image.
> Question: The word "deliberate" in the passage is closest in meaning to
> A. careless
> B. intentional
> C. expensive
> D. traditional

B. The contrast between apparent "errors" and "choices that served the purpose" shows that the painters meant to paint this way. A is the opposite. D might seem reasonable, but it does not fit the idea of choice.
> Question: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
> A. A process is described in the order in which it happens.
> B. A common first impression is presented and then challenged with examples.
> C. Two styles of painting are compared and one is judged better.
> D. A problem is described and several solutions are proposed.

B: the first sentence gives the visitors' impression, "Historians of art see it differently" challenges it, and the examples of the profile view and of size support the new view. D is tempting because "errors" sounds like a problem, but no solutions are proposed.
! In organization questions, look for turning-point words such as "However", "see it differently" or "In contrast". They divide the passage into its parts.
## Common traps
- Options that copy long phrases from the passage but change one key relationship (cause becomes effect, before becomes after, some becomes all).
- Too narrow main-idea options that describe only one example.
- Too extreme options with best, always, never, only, completely.
- Outside knowledge: an option that is true in real life but not stated in the passage.
- In EXCEPT questions, forgetting to find the one option that is NOT mentioned. Check each option against the text and cross out the three that are there.
- Reference errors: a pronoun usually refers to the nearest noun that makes sense in number and meaning, not always the nearest noun.
## How to practise between mocks

- Read one short academic text every day: textbook introductions, encyclopedia articles, science magazine pieces. After reading, write the main idea in one sentence and list the parts (claim, example, contrast).
- Build academic vocabulary with the flashcards in this app, especially words with several meanings and their synonyms.
- Practise signal words: make a list grouped by function (contrast, addition, cause, result, example) and notice them as you read.

- After each practice set, classify every mistake by question type. If most mistakes are inference or purpose questions, practise asking "what job does this sentence do?" for every sentence in a paragraph.
- Do not reread the whole passage for every question; train yourself to go straight to the right place using your mental map.
